e.t: This word means “singing” or “to sing,” describing the act of expressing words or praise through song. It functions as an action word, pointing to vocal music rather than merely speaking. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times: twice in instructions involving singing and three times in Revelation’s scenes of heavenly song. Its basic meaning remains consistent across these uses, while the surrounding verse determines who is singing and what is being sung.

me: Adjective, Accusative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word describes someone who is beyond reproach or not condemned. It points to a life or conduct that cannot rightly be charged with blame. In ordinary Bible language, it expresses an upright condition that avoids giving legitimate grounds for accusation. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in Titus 2:8, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: conduct that stands free from valid condemnation.

e.t: This word means “be exactly” or “to find out exactly,” expressing careful, precise inquiry rather than a rough guess. It describes getting accurate information or determining something with exactness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Matthew chapter 2. Its use presents exact knowledge as the result of deliberate investigation, while the surrounding passage determines what information is being sought. The word therefore emphasizes precision and certainty in finding something out.

This word describes a meddler—someone who improperly involves himself in matters that do not belong to him. It points to intrusive interference rather than faithful service or responsible concern. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in 1 Peter 4:15, so its precise force there must be understood from that verse’s surrounding context. The word’s central idea remains clear: becoming entangled in another person’s affairs in a wrongful or unwelcome way.

e.t: This word means “to sigh deeply.” It describes an audible or expressed sigh rather than speech, naming the act itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 8:12, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse is not included here. The word focuses on the deep sigh as an action. Its exact force in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage and the speaker’s situation.

It distinguishes what is human from what is divine or heavenly, though the precise emphasis depends on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, including several uses in 1 Corinthians. Its basic force remains focused on human limitation, origin, or involvement rather than on an abstract or purely spiritual source.

The emphasis is on purposeful defense rather than a general feeling of protection. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, including passages in Luke, Acts, Romans, and 2 Corinthians. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on who is being defended and on the surrounding words.

The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 11:53. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to sustained questioning rather than a single simple inquiry.

In the supplied Greek New Testament corpus, it occurs once, so its meaning is narrowly focused: it names one person. The reference establishes where the word appears, while the surrounding wording would be needed to explain that passage’s fuller significance.

e.t: Gehenna is a distinct name used in the New Testament, normally retained in English rather than replaced by a descriptive translation. It occurs twelve times in twelve New Testament verses, beginning in Matthew and continuing through James. The word itself identifies Gehenna, while its fuller significance in a particular passage must be understood from the surrounding scriptural context. Its repeated use shows that it is an established biblical term, not a general adjective or action word.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 13 times, especially in Matthew and Mark. The word identifies the person’s condition rather than naming a demon or explaining every detail of the situation. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and account.

It can describe someone who has stayed, something that continues to exist, or a person who persists over time. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, with the English rendering “remained” appearing more than once. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what person or thing is said to remain. It expresses cleansing as an action rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, so its basic meaning is clear even though its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. Scripture uses it in 1 Corinthians and 2 Timothy.

e.t: This word describes someone as “to be covered with sores” or “to have sores.” It focuses on the condition of having sores rather than naming a sore itself. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 16:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: a person is afflicted with sores or is in a state marked by them.

It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 21:7. Its basic meaning remains focused on the physical act of sitting; the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being sat on and how the action fits the scene.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages translated with “obtained” and “obtain.” Its precise force in any one verse depends on what is being sought or received in that surrounding passage.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “clothing,” referring to garments worn on the body. It describes what someone is dressed in rather than an action or inner quality. The word occurs eight times in seven New Testament verses, showing a straightforward reference to apparel in different settings. Its ordinary sense remains concrete: the visible garments a person wears. In each passage, the surrounding verse supplies the particular situation, but the word itself simply identifies clothing.

e.t: This word means “differently” or “otherwise.” It is an adverb, describing a different manner or an alternative way of thinking or acting. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 3:15. Its basic sense points to a difference from what has just been stated or from an expected way of proceeding. The surrounding verse and passage determine precisely how that difference functions there.

e.t: This word means “rope,” referring to a strong cord used for tying, securing, or handling something. It is a concrete noun describing a physical object rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:40. Its basic meaning remains simple and specific: a rope. The surrounding verse provides the context for exactly how the rope functions there, but the word itself names the object.

e.t: This word means a marvel or wonder—something that prompts astonishment and amazement. It refers to a remarkable matter that causes people to marvel rather than to an ordinary event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, with English renderings expressing both “marvel” and “wonder.” Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains a response of amazement to something extraordinary.

e.t: This word means “camel,” referring to the large animal known in the Bible. It is used as a noun for the animal itself or for something belonging to it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, appearing in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its uses include references to a camel’s clothing and to a camel in Jesus’ teaching. The surrounding verse determines the exact point being made in each occurrence.

e.t: “Mutilation” refers to the damaging or cutting of the body, and this word names that act rather than a person or object. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Philippians 3:2. Its central sense is physical injury produced by cutting. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context; its lexical meaning remains “mutilation.”

e.t: This word means “ark”: a large chest or vessel used to hold and preserve what is inside. In the Greek New Testament, it refers to the ark connected with Noah and to the sacred ark associated with God’s covenant, so its exact reference depends on the passage. It occurs six times, appearing in Matthew, Luke, Hebrews, 1 Peter, and Revelation. The word consistently identifies an ark rather than describing an action or quality.

Korah is a personal name, referring to a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name appears once, in Jude 1:11. The form rendered “Korah’s” identifies something associated with Korah, while the name itself remains a proper name. The supplied record does not include the verse text, so the specific point Jude makes about Korah must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in John 6, identifying the loaves involved in the feeding of the multitude and the pieces gathered afterward. The word therefore points specifically to barley bread or loaves rather than wheat bread. Its basic meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding passage supplies the larger significance of the event.

Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its central idea remains authority or lordship. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 20:28 and Mark 10:45, and is rendered “ransom” in both places. The precise force of the word in either verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a ransom given for release.

Its precise force in any sentence depends on what word, name, or saying is being clarified.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Acts. The word appears in accounts involving different young men, so its basic meaning remains consistent while the surrounding passage determines each person’s particular role. It describes the person himself, not a spiritual quality or character trait.

It identifies a recognized role connected with the temple rather than the temple building itself. In the Greek New Testament, the word occurs once, in Acts 19:35. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to a temple guardian or guard.

This word means “who,” “which,” or “who/which.” It points back to a person or thing and connects that person or thing with further information in the sentence. Its meaning depends on whether the sentence refers to people or things, so it may describe either. This Greek New Testament word occurs 144 times, showing that it serves a common connecting function across many passages rather than expressing a separate doctrine or spiritual concept.

Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is simply the proper name Pontius.

It presents an action as plunging forward rather than proceeding carefully or upright. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 1:18, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains a vivid description of someone or something going headlong.

The word expresses abandonment directed toward the speaker, but the precise force of the statement in each passage belongs to the surrounding verse and context. Its basic meaning remains a direct declaration that someone has been forsaken.

The word itself identifies the body part rather than an attitude, action, or spiritual quality.
